blocks.text: **Acromegaly** is the clinical syndrome caused by **excess growth hormone (GH)** in an adult, nearly always secreted by an anterior **pituitary adenoma** (Davidson: usually a macroadenoma). Once the epiphyses have fused, GH can no longer lengthen bones, so the skeleton and soft tissues **broaden**. Left untreated, acromegaly carries about **twice the expected mortality**.

blocks.title: Gigantism vs acromegaly
rows: Adult life, after the epiphyses have closed
Excessive linear growth → very tall stature
Broadening of bones and soft tissues (face, jaw, hands, feet)
Rare; relatively more frequent in familial (AIP) disease
The usual presentation of GH excess
Excess beginning in adolescence and continuing into adult life gives features of both

blocks.title: The GH–IGF-1 axis
items: GH is released by somatotrophs in **pulses** under dual hypothalamic control: **GHRH stimulates**, **somatostatin inhibits**.
**Ghrelin**, made in the stomach, is an additional stimulus to GH release.
GH binds a single-transmembrane receptor, mainly in the **liver**, which signals through the **JAK/STAT** pathway.
Most growth effects are indirect, via **IGF-1** produced in the liver and other tissues; GH also acts directly on liver, muscle, bone and fat.
GH increases protein and collagen synthesis and **opposes insulin** (a counter-regulatory hormone).
IGF-1 exerts **negative feedback** on the hypothalamus and pituitary.
**Dopamine** also restrains GH release, though less potently than somatostatin; both pathways are exploited by drug therapy.

blocks.text: GH is **pulsatile**, so one high random GH value does not confirm acromegaly. Prolactin, in contrast, is not pulsatile, so a random level is enough to diagnose hyperprolactinaemia.
Because GH is an **insulin antagonist**, GH excess is a recognised cause of **secondary diabetes**.

blocks.note: Look at: GHRH (+) and somatostatin (−) acting on the pituitary, GH driving hepatic IGF-1, and IGF-1 feeding back on hypothalamus and pituitary.

blocks.text: Acromegaly is **rare**: incidence roughly 3–4 per million per year and prevalence 50–80 per million. Men and women are affected equally, with a peak in **middle age**, and most cases are **sporadic**.

blocks.title: Causes of GH excess
items: **Somatotroph (GH-secreting) pituitary adenoma**: benign, responsible for almost every case; sometimes linked to specific G-protein mutations.
**Mixed GH + prolactin adenoma**: lactotrophs and somatotrophs share a common cell lineage, so some tumours (even some prolactinomas) secrete both hormones.
**Familial isolated pituitary adenoma** (usually _AIP_ gene mutation): onset is more often before puberty, so gigantism is commoner than in sporadic disease.
**MEN 1**: pituitary adenomas in about 70% (prolactinoma, GH- or ACTH-secreting); pancreatic islet tumours may secrete GH-releasing factor.
**McCune–Albright syndrome** (mostly girls): precocious puberty, polyostotic fibrous dysplasia and café-au-lait patches; pituitary hypersecretion may cause acromegaly or gigantism.
**Ectopic GHRH** (rarely GH itself) from a lung or pancreatic tumour: very rare; ectopic GHRH causes pituitary **hyperplasia** rather than an adenoma.

blocks.title: Classifying pituitary adenomas
rows: > 10 mm diameter (usual size of a GH tumour at diagnosis)

blocks.text: Shared lineage explains two exam links: about **30% of acromegalics have raised prolactin** (co-secretion), and dopamine agonists work best in **mixed GH/prolactin** tumours.

Quick sources disagree on how many pituitary adenomas secrete GH (Step-Up: about one-third; Pocket Medicine: about 10%). Avoid basing an answer on this figure; the examinable point is that GH excess is **almost always a pituitary adenoma**.

Features come from two sources: **local tumour effects** (headache, visual field loss, cranial nerve palsy, hypopituitarism) and **systemic effects of GH/IGF-1 excess** (sweating, soft tissue and bony overgrowth, metabolic change). Onset is **insidious**, and diagnosis often comes years after symptoms begin.

Davidson lists **headache and sweating** as the commonest complaints. Kumar notes that about a third of patients present with a **change in appearance** and about a quarter with headache or visual field loss; the rest are picked up by an alert doctor in another clinic (general practice, diabetes, hypertension, dental or dermatology).

blocks.title: Features by region
rows: Prominent supraorbital ridges / frontal bossing (large frontal sinuses), prognathism, interdental separation, enlarged nose and lips, macroglossia, coarse features, deep voice
Spade-like hands and feet, tight rings, increasing glove/ring/shoe size, thick heel pads, carpal tunnel syndrome
Excess sweating, thick greasy skin, hirsutism, skin tags and acanthosis
Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, impotence or low libido, features of hypopituitarism, goitre
Tiredness, weight gain, joint pain, proximal myopathy, hypertension, enlarged liver and other organs, glycosuria, snoring / sleep apnoea
Headache; bitemporal hemianopia or upper quadrantanopia; diplopia from 3rd, 4th or 6th nerve palsy if the tumour invades the cavernous sinus

blocks.title: Signs printed in bold as most discriminating (Kumar/KC figures)
items: **Prognathism** (protruding lower jaw)
**Interdental separation**
**Large tongue** (macroglossia)
**Spade-like hands and feet**
Other listed signs (supraorbital ridge, tight rings, carpal tunnel, greasy skin, field defects) are useful but not highlighted

blocks.title: Direction of tumour spread
items: **Upwards** → optic chiasm compression → bitemporal hemianopia
**Laterally** → cavernous sinus → 3rd/4th/6th nerve palsy and diplopia
**Downwards** → invasion of the sphenoid sinus

blocks.text: In the history, ask about **ring, glove and shoe size**. **Sweating, headache and soft tissue swelling** are the best markers of ongoing GH activity; headache can be severe even with a small tumour and often settles after surgery or somatostatin analogues.

blocks.note: Look at: supraorbital ridges, prognathism, enlarged lips/nose/tongue, large hands and feet with thick heel pads, plus labelled complications.
Look at: the photographs of prognathism and of acromegalic hands with spade-like soft tissue enlargement.

blocks.text: Diagnosis is **biochemical first, imaging second**. Davidson confirms acromegaly by showing that GH **fails to suppress during an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)** together with a **raised IGF-1**. Imaging comes only after biochemistry is abnormal.

blocks.title: Key investigations
rows: Almost always raised; reflects mean 24-hour GH and fluctuates little
Useful in diagnosis; a normal IGF-1 is strong evidence against acromegaly
No suppression (normal nadir < 0.5 μg/L ≈ 2 mIU/L); paradoxical rise in about 30%
Pulsatile, so a detectable value is non-diagnostic
Only an undetectable level helps (it excludes)
Almost always shows the adenoma, usually a macroadenoma
Do it after the biochemistry is abnormal
Bitemporal hemianopia if the chiasm is compressed
Partial or complete hypopituitarism is common
May suggest benefit from a dopamine agonist
IGT or diabetes; raised triglycerides and phosphate
Kumar: about 25% have a diabetic GTT
Part of the work-up in Davidson

blocks.text: OGTT cut-offs vary by book and assay. **Davidson (use this):** normal GH suppresses to **< 0.5 μg/L (≈ 2 mIU/L)**. Kumar: acromegalics fail to suppress below 0.3 μg/L. Quick sources: < 1 ng/mL (< 0.3 with newer assays) or < 1 mU/L. The concept to remember is **failure of suppression, sometimes with a paradoxical rise**.
MRI shows pituitary "abnormalities" in up to **10% of healthy middle-aged people**, so scanning before biochemistry invites false positives.
In acromegaly, prolactin is **normal or raised**, never characteristically low. A low prolactin offered as a feature in an MCQ is a distractor.

blocks.note: Look at: a small lucent intrasellar microadenoma vs a macroadenoma pressing on the optic chiasm and cavernous sinus, and a macroadenoma with massive suprasellar extension.
Look at: MRI of a microadenoma (< 10 mm) and a macroadenoma (> 10 mm), plus the acromegaly clues (headache, sweating, change in shoe and ring size).

blocks.title: Complications of acromegaly
rows: Hypertension, LVH / cardiomyopathy, heart failure, coronary disease
Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death; risk raised 2–3-fold
Impaired glucose tolerance (~25%), type 2 diabetes (~10%), hyperphosphataemia
Colonic polyps and colorectal cancer (risk raised 2–3-fold)
Acromegaly is a recognised risk factor for colorectal cancer
Submucosal soft-tissue thickening narrows the upper airway
Arthropathy (~50%), mechanical back pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, proximal myopathy, Raynaud's
From the tumour itself or its treatment

blocks.text: **Acromegalic arthropathy** mainly affects large joints. It looks like osteoarthritis, but the range of movement is **normal or increased**. X-rays show **widened joint spaces, squared bone ends, generalised osteopenia and tufting of the terminal phalanges**. It does **not** improve once the acromegaly is treated.

**Prognosis:** untreated acromegaly shortens survival substantially. Most deaths are from **heart failure, coronary artery disease and hypertension-related causes**, and deaths from neoplasia (especially large-bowel tumours) are also increased. Bringing GH down to a "safe" level with a normal IGF-1 returns mortality towards normal.
Sleep apnoea is common in acromegaly. Ask about snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness, and investigate if they are present.
Glucose-intolerance figures differ: **Davidson: IGT ~25%, type 2 diabetes ~10%** (use these); Kumar: about 25% have a diabetic GTT; Step-Up: 10–15% have glucose intolerance or diabetes.

Goals: **relieve symptoms** and **normalise GH and IGF-1** to cut morbidity and mortality. Kumar advises treating everyone except the elderly or those with minimal abnormalities. Also **correct hypopituitarism** and treat diabetes and hypertension, which usually improve once GH is controlled.

blocks.alt: Stepwise management: trans-sphenoidal surgery first; reassess with imaging, OGTT GH and IGF-1; if persistent, somatostatin analogue with or without dopamine agonist; if still uncontrolled add pegvisomant; external radiotherapy is second line with drugs bridging its slow effect.

blocks.title: Treatment options (Davidson Box 18.57: surgery 1st line; radiotherapy and drugs 2nd line)
rows: May cure, especially microadenomas (remission 60–90%) but only ~50% of macroadenomas; often just debulks. ~10% recur. Very high pre-op GH/IGF-1 predicts lower cure. Risks: hypopituitarism, diabetes insipidus, CSF rhinorrhoea, infection
2nd line; also primary or pre-operative therapy
Act on SSTR2/SSTR5; slow-release injections every few weeks (monthly depot); modest shrinkage in some; gallstones and high cost; not all reach target
Oral; less effective than somatostatin analogues; best in mixed GH/prolactin tumours; doses higher than for prolactinoma (cabergoline 0.5 mg daily, bromocriptine 10–60 mg daily)
When GH/IGF-1 stay high on somatostatin analogues
GH receptor antagonist (blocks receptor dimerisation); daily self-injection; normalises IGF-1 but does not lower GH or shrink the tumour
2nd line for persistent disease after surgery
GH falls slowly over years (Kumar: possibly 10 years or more), so drugs bridge the gap; hypopituitarism in 50–70% within 10 years; unsuitable when urgent treatment is needed
Reserved for suprasellar or massive tumours

blocks.title: Follow-up after treatment
items: Retest pituitary function **4–6 weeks** after surgery to detect new deficits.
Repeat pituitary imaging after **3–6 months**; post-operative imaging and the OGTT guide further therapy.
After radiotherapy, **annual pituitary function tests** are obligatory.
Regular **colonoscopy** to find and remove polyps is advised, although evidence of benefit is inconclusive.
Track control with GH and IGF-1 (IGF-1 alone on pegvisomant).

blocks.text: If the GH excess comes from **ectopic GHRH or GH** secreted by a lung or pancreatic tumour, treatment is removal of that tumour.

Treatment GH targets differ. **Davidson (use this): GH < 1.0 μg/L (≈ 3 mIU/L) with a normal IGF-1.** Kumar: mean GH < 2.5 μg/L ("safe" level). KC Essentials: < 5 mU/L. All sources also require an age-adjusted normal IGF-1.
**Pegvisomant** blocks the GH receptor, so serum GH does not fall even when the disease is controlled. **Monitor IGF-1, not GH**, and do not expect the tumour to shrink.
Unlike dopamine agonists in prolactinoma, medical therapy in acromegaly **does not reliably shrink macroadenomas**. Inoperable tumours are treated with radiotherapy plus medical therapy.

cards.front: Gigantism vs acromegaly: what decides which develops?
cards.back: Timing of GH excess relative to **epiphyseal fusion**: before fusion → gigantism (tall stature); after → acromegaly (broadening of bone and soft tissue).
**GHRH** stimulates, **somatostatin** inhibits; ghrelin also stimulates; IGF-1 feeds back negatively.

cards.front: Why is a single random GH unhelpful in diagnosing acromegaly?
cards.back: GH is secreted in **pulses**, so a high random level does not confirm disease (only an undetectable level helps exclude it).
A benign **GH-secreting (somatotroph) pituitary adenoma**, usually a macroadenoma.

cards.front: Gene linked to familial acromegaly with more gigantism?
cards.back: **AIP** (familial isolated pituitary adenoma): earlier, pre-pubertal onset.
Precocious puberty, **polyostotic fibrous dysplasia**, café-au-lait patches (may include GH excess).

cards.front: Classic visual field defect from a GH macroadenoma?
cards.back: **Bitemporal hemianopia** (or upper quadrantanopia) from optic chiasm compression.

cards.front: Which blood test fluctuates less than GH and, if normal, argues strongly against acromegaly?
cards.back: **Serum IGF-1**: almost always raised in acromegaly and reflects mean 24-hour GH.

cards.front: Confirmatory test and the abnormal result (Davidson)?
cards.back: GH during an **OGTT**: GH fails to suppress below 0.5 μg/L (≈ 2 mIU/L); paradoxical rise in ~30%.

cards.front: Proportion of acromegalics with raised prolactin?
Leading cause of death in acromegaly?
cards.back: **Cardiovascular disease**: heart failure, coronary disease, hypertension-related causes.
Widened joint spaces, squared bone ends, osteopenia, **tufting of terminal phalanges**; does not improve after treatment.

cards.front: Which cancer is increased in acromegaly, and how is it screened?
Davidson's biochemical target on medical therapy?
cards.back: GH **< 1.0 μg/L (≈ 3 mIU/L)** and a normal IGF-1.
GH receptor antagonist (daily injection); GH stays high, so **monitor IGF-1**.
More **gallstones** and high cost; given as depot injections.

cards.front: Hypopituitarism risk after fractionated pituitary radiotherapy?
cards.back: **50–70% within 10 years**: annual pituitary function tests are obligatory.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old boy is referred because his height is far above the 99th centile and well above his parents' heights. He has grown 12 cm in the past year, sweats heavily and has needed three larger pairs of shoes this year. A hand X-ray shows open epiphyses. Serum IGF-1 is markedly raised.
questions.leadIn: Which term best describes his condition?
questions.explanation: GH excess that starts **before the epiphyses fuse** drives excessive linear growth: **gigantism**. The raised IGF-1, sweating and rapid acral growth point to GH excess; the open epiphyses show he can still grow taller.
whyNot: Acromegaly is GH excess after epiphyseal fusion, causing broadening rather than height gain.
Laron dwarfism is GH resistance, which causes short stature, not tall stature.
Familial tall stature would not explain a markedly raised IGF-1 with sweating and acral overgrowth.
Sex-steroid-driven growth would not explain a markedly raised IGF-1 with sweating and soft tissue overgrowth.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with acromegaly starts monthly depot injections of lanreotide. Over three months her GH and IGF-1 concentrations fall.
questions.leadIn: Lanreotide is a synthetic analogue of which endogenous hormone?
questions.explanation: GH is under dual hypothalamic control: GHRH stimulates and **somatostatin inhibits**. Octreotide and lanreotide are somatostatin analogues acting on SSTR2 and SSTR5 receptors on the tumour.
whyNot: GHRH stimulates GH release; an analogue would worsen acromegaly.
Ghrelin from the stomach stimulates GH release.
Dopamine weakly inhibits GH, but it is mimicked by oral cabergoline or bromocriptine, not lanreotide.
IGF-1 is the downstream mediator of GH and is already in excess.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is diagnosed with acromegaly. He has had two episodes of renal colic, and his serum calcium and PTH are both raised. Five years ago he was treated for recurrent duodenal ulcers associated with a very high fasting gastrin.
questions.leadIn: Which underlying condition is most likely?
options: Ectopic GHRH secretion from a lung tumour
questions.explanation: Pituitary (GH) adenoma + primary hyperparathyroidism + gastrinoma (Zollinger–Ellison) = the classic **pituitary, parathyroid and pancreas** tumours of **MEN 1**. Pituitary adenomas occur in about 70% of patients with MEN 1.
whyNot: MEN 2a (RET mutation) does not include pituitary adenomas or gastrinomas.
McCune–Albright presents in childhood with precocious puberty, fibrous dysplasia and café-au-lait patches.
Ectopic GHRH would not explain hyperparathyroidism and gastrinoma.
A sporadic adenoma would not explain tumours in the parathyroid and pancreas.

questions.stem: A pituitary tumour removed by trans-sphenoidal surgery from a 50-year-old man with acromegaly is examined with conventional histological stains.
questions.leadIn: Which appearance is most typical of this tumour?
questions.explanation: On classical staining, GH- and prolactin-secreting adenomas are typically **acidophil**. Somatotroph adenomas are usually acidophil.
whyNot: Basophil adenomas typically secrete ACTH (Cushing's disease).
Chromophobe adenomas are usually non-functioning.
Hypophysitis is an inflammatory cause of hypopituitarism, not of GH excess.
Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke's pouch remnants and does not secrete GH.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best-fitting option in the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.
questions.theme: Clinical findings in a GH-secreting pituitary tumour

items.stem: A 46-year-old man has a raised IGF-1. For 6 months he has woken at night with tingling in his thumb, index and middle fingers, relieved by shaking his hand. Tapping over the flexor retinaculum reproduces it.
items.explanation: Median nerve compression at the wrist, caused by soft tissue overgrowth: **carpal tunnel syndrome**, a recognised sign of acromegaly.

items.stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her dentist that gaps have appeared between her lower front teeth over 2 years. Her jaw now juts forward, and her IGF-1 is raised.
items.explanation: Mandibular growth (prognathism) spreads the teeth apart: **interdental separation**, one of the signs with greatest discriminant value.

items.stem: A 49-year-old man with a GH-secreting macroadenoma sees double when looking to the left. MRI shows the tumour extending laterally beside the sella.
items.explanation: Two steps: lateral extension → the **cavernous sinus**, which carries the 3rd, 4th and 6th cranial nerves. Diplopia on lateral gaze fits a **6th nerve palsy**.

items.stem: A 38-year-old woman with acromegaly has oligomenorrhoea and milky nipple discharge. Her serum prolactin is moderately raised.
items.explanation: About 30% of GH tumours co-secrete prolactin (shared cell lineage), which explains **galactorrhoea** and menstrual disturbance.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best-fitting option in the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.
options: GH measured during an oral glucose tolerance test

items.stem: A GP sees a 44-year-old man whose wife thinks his face has coarsened. She wants one blood test to screen for GH excess, which reflects mean 24-hour GH and changes little during the day.
items.explanation: **IGF-1** integrates GH secretion over the day and is almost always raised in acromegaly; a normal value argues strongly against it.

items.stem: A 51-year-old woman with sweating, headaches and enlarging hands has a raised IGF-1. The endocrinologist wants the test that confirms the diagnosis.
items.explanation: Confirm with **GH during an OGTT**: in acromegaly GH fails to suppress (normal nadir < 0.5 μg/L), and about 30% show a paradoxical rise.

items.stem: A 47-year-old man has confirmed biochemical acromegaly. The team now wants to show the source of the GH and plan surgery.
items.explanation: Once biochemistry is abnormal, **MRI pituitary** almost always shows the adenoma. Imaging before that risks incidental findings.

items.stem: MRI in a 55-year-old man with acromegaly shows a macroadenoma with suprasellar extension touching the optic chiasm. He has not noticed any visual problem.
items.explanation: Chiasmal compression can cause an unnoticed bitemporal hemianopia; **formal perimetry** documents it and guides urgency.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing acromegaly has aching knees and hips. The joints are crepitant but move through a **full or slightly increased** range. X-rays show widened joint spaces, squared-off bone ends, osteopenia and tufting of the terminal phalanges.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: **Acromegalic arthropathy** (about 50%) mainly affects large joints and resembles OA, but range of movement is preserved or increased and joint spaces **widen** rather than narrow. It does not improve once acromegaly is treated.
whyNot: Primary OA narrows joint spaces and restricts movement.
RA is an inflammatory, mainly small-joint arthritis with erosions, not widened joint spaces and phalangeal tufting.
Pyrophosphate arthropathy shows chondrocalcinosis, not widened joint spaces with phalangeal tufting.
Paget's disease causes bone expansion and deformity, not widened joint spaces with phalangeal tufting.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with newly confirmed acromegaly asks why treatment is recommended when her main symptom is sweating.
questions.leadIn: Which group of conditions accounts for most deaths in untreated acromegaly?
questions.explanation: Untreated acromegaly roughly doubles mortality, mostly from **heart failure, coronary disease and hypertension-related causes** (cardiomyopathy).
whyNot: Colorectal cancer deaths are increased but are not the main cause of death.
Apoplexy is a rare acute event, not the main cause of death.
Diabetes is common, but hyperglycaemic crises are not the main cause of death.
Sleep apnoea is common but contributes far less to mortality than cardiovascular disease.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best-fitting option in the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.
options: Resection of an extrapituitary GHRH-secreting tumour

items.stem: A fit 40-year-old woman has newly confirmed acromegaly. MRI shows a 7 mm adenoma confined to the sella.
items.explanation: **Trans-sphenoidal surgery** is first line and is most likely to cure a microadenoma (remission 60–90%).

items.stem: A 52-year-old man still has a raised IGF-1 after surgery and 12 months of maximal-dose octreotide depot.
items.explanation: **Pegvisomant**, a GH receptor antagonist, is used when GH/IGF-1 stay high despite somatostatin analogues.

items.stem: A 45-year-old woman has mild residual disease after surgery. Her tumour stained for both GH and prolactin, and she would prefer a tablet to injections.
items.explanation: Dopamine agonists are oral and work best in **mixed GH/prolactin** tumours, useful for mild residual disease: **cabergoline**.

items.stem: A 60-year-old man has acromegaly with diffuse pituitary enlargement but no discrete adenoma. CT shows a mass in the pancreas, and plasma GHRH is high.
items.explanation: Two steps: hyperplasia without an adenoma plus a raised GHRH means **ectopic GHRH**. Treatment is removal of the source tumour.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best-fitting option in the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.

items.stem: A 41-year-old woman with vague tiredness has a single random serum GH of 3.5 μg/L taken in clinic. No other GH axis tests have been done.
items.explanation: GH is pulsatile, so a detectable random GH is **non-diagnostic**; check IGF-1 and do an OGTT if needed.

items.stem: A 48-year-old man with sweating and enlarging hands has a raised IGF-1. During an OGTT his GH rises from 3.8 to 5.1 μg/L.
items.explanation: GH should fall below 0.5 μg/L. Failure to suppress (here a **paradoxical rise**, seen in ~30%) with a raised IGF-1 **confirms acromegaly**.

items.stem: Six months after surgery, a 55-year-old woman on lanreotide has a mean GH of 0.7 μg/L and an IGF-1 within the age-adjusted range.
items.explanation: Davidson's targets are GH < 1.0 μg/L (≈ 3 mIU/L) with a normal IGF-1, so this is **biochemical control**.

items.stem: A 46-year-old man on octreotide depot after surgery has a mean GH of 2.2 μg/L, and his IGF-1 remains above the age-adjusted range.
items.explanation: A raised IGF-1 means **persistent active disease**, whatever the GH. Davidson's GH target is < 1.0 μg/L. Kumar's "safe" GH of < 2.5 μg/L would not make this controlled either, because IGF-1 must also be normal.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man attends with a change in appearance noticed by his family. You suspect a pituitary cause.
questions.leadIn: According to Davidson, which pair of complaints is most common in acromegaly?
questions.explanation: **Headache and sweating** are the commonest complaints; sweating is also a sensitive marker of ongoing GH activity.
whyNot: Cranial nerve palsies from cavernous sinus invasion are unusual presentations.
These suggest diabetes insipidus or uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.
These suggest thyrotoxicosis.
These suggest Cushing's syndrome.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has frontal bossing, enlarged hands and excessive sweating. You plan his first investigation for suspected acromegaly.
questions.leadIn: Which investigation should be done first?
questions.explanation: Start with **IGF-1**: almost always raised, stable through the day, and a normal value argues strongly against acromegaly. A raised value leads to an OGTT and then MRI.
whyNot: MRI shows "abnormalities" in up to 10% of healthy people, so it follows biochemistry.
Random GH is pulsatile, so a detectable value is non-diagnostic.
Visual fields document mass effect but do not diagnose GH excess.
Biopsy is done only as part of therapeutic surgery.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has persistent GH excess after trans-sphenoidal surgery and is given fractionated external pituitary radiotherapy, with octreotide while it takes effect.
questions.leadIn: Which monitoring is obligatory every year after the radiotherapy?
questions.explanation: Fractionated pituitary radiotherapy carries a lifelong risk of **hypopituitarism (50–70% within 10 years)**, so annual pituitary function testing is mandatory.
whyNot: Cardiac assessment may be needed in acromegaly but is not the obligatory radiotherapy surveillance.
Bone densitometry is not the key surveillance after pituitary radiotherapy.
Hearing loss is not the recognised late effect.
Calcium is not affected by pituitary radiotherapy.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy is 2.05 m tall with large hands and a raised IGF-1. His paternal cousin had a pituitary tumour removed at 17. Genetic testing finds a germline mutation.
questions.leadIn: Which gene is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: **AIP** mutations cause familial isolated pituitary adenoma. Familial disease starts before puberty more often than sporadic disease, so **gigantism** is more prevalent.
whyNot: RET causes MEN 2, which does not feature pituitary adenomas.
MEN 1 would usually bring parathyroid and pancreatic tumours as well, not an isolated pituitary tumour.
McCune–Albright is a sporadic (non-inherited) G-protein mutation with fibrous dysplasia and café-au-lait patches.
VHL causes haemangioblastomas, renal cancer and phaeochromocytoma, not GH adenomas.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best-fitting option in the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.

items.stem: A 54-year-old man with untreated acromegaly has gained weight. His wife reports loud snoring with pauses in breathing, and he falls asleep at his desk. His BMI is 27.
items.explanation: Step 1: snoring, witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness = sleep apnoea. Step 2: a BMI of 27 alone is unlikely to explain it; in acromegaly, **submucosal soft tissue thickening narrows the upper airway**. Answer: **obstructive sleep apnoea**, common in acromegaly and worth investigating.

items.stem: A 49-year-old woman with acromegaly has thirst and polyuria. Fasting plasma glucose is 8.4 mmol/L on two occasions; islet autoantibodies are negative.
items.explanation: Step 1: two fasting glucose values ≥ 7.0 mmol/L with symptoms = diabetes. Step 2: GH is an **insulin antagonist**, so excess GH causes **secondary diabetes**. Davidson: IGT ~25%, type 2 diabetes ~10%. Step 3: it usually improves as GH is controlled.

items.stem: A 61-year-old man treated for acromegaly 10 years ago has a 3-month change in bowel habit and iron-deficiency anaemia.
items.explanation: Step 1: change in bowel habit + iron deficiency in an older adult = suspect a colonic lesion. Step 2: acromegaly raises colorectal cancer risk 2–3-fold and is a listed risk factor. Answer: **colorectal carcinoma**; this is why colonoscopy surveillance is advised.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old man had trans-sphenoidal surgery for a GH-secreting macroadenoma. Three months later his IGF-1 is still raised and GH does not suppress during an OGTT. MRI shows residual tumour within the right cavernous sinus.
questions.leadIn: What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start pegvisomant as the first drug
Observe and repeat IGF-1 in 12 months
questions.explanation: Step 1: persistent disease after surgery (raised IGF-1, no GH suppression). Step 2: residual tumour in the cavernous sinus is rarely resectable, so further surgery is unlikely to help. Step 3: Davidson's second-line options are medical therapy and/or radiotherapy; the usual first drug is a **somatostatin analogue** (octreotide/lanreotide/pasireotide depot), aiming for GH < 1.0 μg/L and a normal IGF-1. Radiotherapy may be added, with the drug bridging its slow effect.
whyNot: Pegvisomant is reserved for patients not controlled on somatostatin analogues.
Craniotomy is for suprasellar or massive tumours; cavernous sinus extensions are rarely resectable.
Dopamine agonists are less effective and need higher doses than in prolactinoma; alone they rarely reach safe GH levels.
Active acromegaly roughly doubles mortality, so it should be treated, not watched.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best-fitting option in the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.
options: Ectopic GHRH from a pancreatic or lung tumour

items.stem: A 7-year-old girl has breast development, irregular café-au-lait patches and several bone lesions on X-ray due to fibrous dysplasia. She is growing fast and her IGF-1 is high.
items.explanation: Precocious puberty + polyostotic fibrous dysplasia + café-au-lait = **McCune–Albright syndrome**, which can include pituitary GH hypersecretion.

items.stem: A 52-year-old man with typical acromegaly has a 14 mm sellar mass on MRI. He has no relevant family history or other endocrine disease, and prolactin is normal.
items.explanation: Most acromegaly is **sporadic**, from a somatotroph adenoma that is usually a macroadenoma (> 10 mm) at diagnosis.

items.stem: A 36-year-old woman has amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, spade-like hands and prognathism. Prolactin is moderately raised and IGF-1 is high.
items.explanation: Somatotrophs and lactotrophs share a lineage; about 30% of GH tumours co-secrete prolactin: a **mixed GH/prolactin adenoma**.

items.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops acromegalic features. MRI shows a uniformly enlarged pituitary without a discrete adenoma. Plasma GHRH is high and CT shows a pancreatic mass.
items.explanation: Two steps: pituitary **hyperplasia** (not adenoma) + high GHRH + an extrapituitary tumour = **ectopic GHRH** secretion, a very rare cause.

questions.leadIn: Match each case below to the best-fitting option in the list. Any option can be the answer for several cases, or for none.

items.stem: A peptide analogue that binds SSTR2 and SSTR5 receptors on the adenoma is given as a monthly depot; it can also be used before surgery.
items.explanation: **Octreotide** (like lanreotide) is a somatostatin analogue acting on SSTR2/SSTR5; drawbacks include gallstones and cost.

items.stem: A daily self-injected drug, a modified GH molecule, stops the GH receptor from dimerising. After starting it, the patient's IGF-1 normalises but serum GH has not fallen.
items.explanation: **Pegvisomant** blocks GH action, not secretion, so GH stays high. Monitor IGF-1.

items.stem: A long-acting oral ergot dopamine agonist is added for a mixed GH/prolactin tumour, at a daily dose higher than used for prolactinoma. Missed doses matter little because of its long half-life.
items.explanation: **Cabergoline** is long-acting (Davidson Box 18.59); in acromegaly Kumar quotes 0.5 mg daily, higher than in prolactinoma.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old woman has had monthly lanreotide injections for acromegaly for 2 years. She now has episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals.
questions.leadIn: Which adverse effect of her treatment best explains this?
questions.explanation: Somatostatin analogues (octreotide, lanreotide) are associated with an **increased incidence of gallstones**; biliary colic after fatty meals fits.
whyNot: Peptic ulcer pain is epigastric and not a recognised effect of somatostatin analogues.
Hepatitis is not the characteristic adverse effect.
Renal colic is loin-to-groin pain, unrelated to meals.
Malabsorption would cause steatorrhoea rather than meal-related right upper quadrant pain.

questions.stem: Thirty-six hours after trans-sphenoidal surgery for acromegaly, a 47-year-old man passes large volumes of very dilute urine and is constantly thirsty. Plasma glucose is normal.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Diabetes insipidus is a recognised complication of pituitary surgery: vasopressin deficiency is usually post-surgical. Lack of vasopressin from the hypothalamus/posterior pituitary is **cranial DI**.
whyNot: Nephrogenic DI is renal resistance to vasopressin (e.g. lithium, hypercalcaemia), not a surgical complication.
Glucose is normal, so there is no osmotic diuresis.
SIADH causes concentrated urine and hyponatraemia, not polyuria.
Primary polydipsia is excess drinking without a vasopressin defect; the surgical timing points to DI.

questions.stem: An endocrine surgeon is counselling patients with newly diagnosed acromegaly about the chance of remission after trans-sphenoidal surgery.
questions.leadIn: Which patient has the best chance of surgical cure?
options: A 6 mm adenoma confined to the sella
A macroadenoma invading the cavernous sinus
A tumour with very high pre-operative GH and IGF-1
A massive macroadenoma with suprasellar extension
A recurrent tumour after previous surgery
questions.explanation: Remission after trans-sphenoidal surgery is **60–90% for microadenomas** but only ~50% for macroadenomas; very high pre-operative GH/IGF-1 predicts a worse result.
whyNot: Cavernous sinus extensions are rarely fully resectable.
Very high pre-operative GH and IGF-1 are poor prognostic markers for cure.
Massive suprasellar tumours may even need transfrontal surgery, and cure rates are low.
Recurrent disease (~10% after surgery) is harder to cure surgically and usually needs second-line therapy.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with acromegaly has loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing at night and daytime sleepiness. His BMI is 26.
questions.leadIn: What is the main mechanism of his breathing disorder?
options: Upper airway narrowing from soft tissue thickening
questions.explanation: Acromegaly predisposes to **obstructive** sleep apnoea because submucosal infiltration and soft tissue enlargement **narrow the upper airway**.
whyNot: Snoring with witnessed obstructive apnoeas points to an upper airway problem, not central hypoventilation.
Cheyne–Stokes breathing is a central pattern of waxing and waning breaths, not snoring with obstruction.
Myopathy is proximal limb weakness, not the cause of sleep apnoea.
Nothing here suggests chest wall deformity.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with acromegaly is not controlled on octreotide and is started on daily pegvisomant injections. Three months later she feels better.
questions.leadIn: Which measurement best shows whether the disease is controlled?
questions.explanation: Pegvisomant blocks GH receptor dimerisation: it **normalises IGF-1 but does not lower GH or shrink the tumour**. So **IGF-1** is the marker of control.
whyNot: GH stays high on pegvisomant, so it cannot judge control.
OGTT GH suppression is also misleading, because GH secretion is unchanged.
Pegvisomant does not shrink the tumour.
Prolactin does not show whether GH action is controlled.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man has just been diagnosed with acromegaly. Apart from pituitary work-up, his endocrinologist arranges one further investigation, since the condition raises the risk of a common cancer 2–3-fold.
questions.leadIn: Which screening investigation is this?
questions.explanation: Acromegaly increases **colonic polyps and colorectal cancer** (2–3-fold); Davidson includes **colonoscopy** in the work-up.
whyNot: Lung cancer risk is not the recognised association.
Breast cancer is not the recognised association.
Goitre can occur, but thyroid cancer screening is not the standard recommendation.
Prostate cancer is not the recognised association.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has 18 months of amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea. She has coarse facial features, spade-like hands and sweats heavily. Serum prolactin is moderately raised and IGF-1 is clearly elevated. MRI shows a 15 mm pituitary adenoma.
questions.leadIn: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A raised IGF-1 with acromegalic features means GH excess; about **30%** of these tumours **co-secrete prolactin** (shared somatotroph–lactotroph lineage), explaining galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea.
whyNot: A pure prolactinoma would not raise IGF-1 or cause acral overgrowth.
Stalk compression can raise prolactin but would not raise IGF-1.
Cushing's disease causes weight gain, bruising, striae and myopathy, not acral growth with high IGF-1.
Hypothyroidism can raise prolactin but does not cause high IGF-1 and spade-like hands.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who hopes to become pregnant still has active acromegaly after trans-sphenoidal surgery. External pituitary radiotherapy is being discussed.
questions.leadIn: Which consequence makes radiotherapy particularly unattractive for her?
questions.explanation: Pituitary radiotherapy often causes **hypopituitarism** (50–70% within 10 years), including gonadotrophin loss, which is why Kumar calls it unattractive in people of reproductive age. Its GH-lowering effect is also slow.
whyNot: Apoplexy is haemorrhage or infarction of a tumour, not the recognised late effect of radiotherapy.
Cranial DI is mainly a surgical complication.
Cataract is not the key concern described for pituitary radiotherapy.
Thyroid cancer is not the recognised consequence.

ospe.identify: Acromegaly: prominent supraorbital ridges (large frontal sinuses), prognathism, enlarged lips/nose/tongue, spade-like hands, large feet with thick heel pads.
Spot diagnosis: **prognathism** (protruding lower jaw), and **spade-like hands** from soft tissue enlargement, both from acromegaly.
Kumar symptom/sign chart: the four signs in bold italic (greatest discriminant value) are **prognathism, interdental separation, large tongue and spade-like hands and feet**.
KC Essentials symptom/sign chart: name the signs printed in bold (greatest discriminant value): **prognathism, interdental separation, large tongue, spade-like hands and feet**.
Pituitary MRI: intrasellar microadenoma vs macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm and cavernous sinus; predict bitemporal hemianopia and possible 3rd/4th/6th nerve palsy.
MRI microadenoma (< 10 mm) vs macroadenoma (> 10 mm); acromegaly clues are headache, sweating, change in shoe/ring size.
Macroadenoma (T) compressing the optic chiasm (C), shrinking after a dopamine agonist. This was a prolactinoma; GH adenomas do not reliably shrink with drugs.
GH–IGF-1 axis: GHRH stimulates and somatostatin inhibits pituitary GH; GH drives hepatic IGF-1; IGF-1 gives negative feedback.
